The user then said: "goals approved; now, dig into the code, and figure out what needs to change, consolidate, fold, clean up, organize, be corrected to get us from where we are to the goal. update the proposal with a concrete plan of action, composed into steps that build inexorably toward the goal." The user then approved page v2, verbatim via Optimize: "approved. proceed." v2 keeps storage order as it is (term order): a one-word key (atom, int, float, pid, ref) is found by word equality, as BEAM does, and order is consulted only to place a new key. Atom ids are not stable, so the v1 decisions on atom order are withdrawn. Page: https://claude.ai/artifact/MmnrdprbWQMF24ejqsUaQL (/Users/j5n/Workspace/fz-map-raw-words.html); measurements https://claude.ai/artifact/KASxGisqvtZNq498dbRi8D. User direction: meet or exceed BEAM in all cases; hand-written optimal arm64 first, then make the compiler emit it. Builder: Optimize. Pass rules are judged on bench and pre-registered on the page.

Step 2. key_order(word, kind, word, kind) works as follows:
- Identical words are equal.
- Integers compare signed.
- Atoms compare by a stored 8-byte name prefix, then by name.
- Binaries compare via Bin::cmp. The seam with fz-9e2.5 is unchanged: Bin { ptr, bit_len } carries eq and cmp in runtime/src/bits.rs, and whoever builds first lands both methods.
- Anything else goes to the general comparator, which validates once at its public entry.

Every site that orders map keys calls key_order. Storage order stays term order, so the compiler's literal pre-sort, map compare, struct-as-map alignment and lib/map.fz docs are unchanged.
title: Two map keys are ordered from their stored words, in term order
